title: Human populations and sharing the biosphere — video support
purpose: Interpret demographic and resource-use evidence while distinguishing population size, per-person use and environmental effects.
fallback: Total resource demand depends on both the number of people and the amount used per person, along with technology and the type of resource. A smaller population with high per-person use can have greater total demand for a particular resource than a larger population with lower use. For example, a hypothetical group of 1000 people using 3 units each demands 3000 units, while 2000 people using 1 unit each demand 2000 units. This simple accounting does not describe every environmental impact, but it shows why head count alone is insufficient. Resource extraction, waste and land-use change can affect habitat, species interactions and population connectivity. The mechanisms and measurements must be specified for the case.

title: Life-history strategies and biotic potential — video support
purpose: Compare life-history patterns as a continuum and interpret survivorship without treating categories as rigid rules.
fallback: The r-associated end of a teaching continuum often includes early reproduction, many small offspring, short generation times and less investment in each offspring. Such traits can support rapid increase when conditions permit. The K-associated end often includes later reproduction, fewer offspring, longer lives and more investment per offspring. These are broad comparisons, not fixed laws that predict every trait or graph for every species. Some organisms combine features from both ends. Sea turtles, for example, produce many eggs yet can be long-lived as adults. Interpret the actual traits supplied rather than forcing every organism into a perfect category.

title: Feeding relationships and predator–prey changes — video support
purpose: Trace energy transfer and interpret predator–prey patterns without assuming correlation proves a single cause.
fallback: When prey become more abundant, predators may have greater feeding success. Improved survival and reproduction can increase predator numbers after a delay. More predators can then contribute to increased prey mortality. A prey decline can later reduce predator reproduction or survival. Such feedback can contribute to oscillating patterns, but real populations are also affected by resources, disease, weather, migration and other interactions. Do not expect the peaks of both populations to occur at exactly the same time. A delay can arise because producing and raising offspring takes time.

title: Mutualism, commensalism and parasitism — video support
purpose: Use benefit, harm and no detected effect to classify close interspecific relationships.
fallback: A mutualistic pollination case can provide food to a pollinator and transfer pollen for a plant. An epiphyte can gain physical support on a tree without taking nourishment from the tree; when no appreciable host effect is established, the model is commensalism. A parasite obtains resources from a host and imposes a cost. A tick feeding on a host is a familiar example. Parasites need not immediately kill the host, and the severity of harm varies. Name the resource or service and explain the effect on each partner. A label alone does not show that you understand the interaction.

title: Primary and secondary succession — video support
purpose: Distinguish primary and secondary succession and explain changing community composition without assuming one inevitable endpoint.
fallback: Early colonizers can change a site by adding organic material, influencing soil conditions or altering light and moisture. Those changes can permit some later species and make conditions less suitable for others. Competition, dispersal and interactions also influence which populations establish. Not every later species is simply “better” than an earlier one; it may be favoured by different conditions. The community can become more structurally complex, but disturbance can interrupt or redirect the sequence. Local climate, available colonists and landform affect the pathway.
